text: ONE GIANT
LEAP
"THAT'S one small step for man, one giant leap for
mankind". Thus astronaut Neil Armstrong as he
stepped on to the moon and into history yesterday.
For a moment the phlegmatic commander of Apollo-11
could be poetic before he retreated again to the
language of the technician. "The surface is fine and
powdery", he told a watching world in a fitting practical
climax to an historic journey: Apollo-11 and the nine
similar craft that will follow it to the moon are among
the greatest successes of technical civilisation yet.
Equally they are a product of the poetic roots of
mankind. The moonfall of Apollo-11 yesterday
morning and the disembarkation first of Armstrong
then of his companion Edwin Aldrin were the
culmination of a dream centuries old, an expectation
of a few decades, the concerted plan of a great nation
for a mere eight years. This world and its neighbour
will never be the same again: a truism that has more
significance now than most other times it has been used.
The moon provided a landmark in history yesterday
but until now it has been a barrier, a goal that has
appeared impossible. Now man has attained it — at
least he has set foot on it and he has a respectable
chance of returning safely — and his sights will be
raised.
To its credit the US Administration has provided
Armstrong and Aldrin with a remarkably unchauvinistic
plaque to leave behind them. They have reinforced the
international aspect of their journey by carrying with
them medals awarded to two dead Soviet cosmonauts.
Yet the universality of yesterday's experience, enhanced
by the remarkable quality of the television reception,
cannot alter the fact that Apollo-11 is a vessel of the
United States and that its triumph is most particularly
a triumph for the American people. President Nixon gave
this fact added emphasis by his entirely understandable
participation in the event via television and a radio link
with the astronauts. The US Congress had gone further
by insisting that no flag but that of the US be carried
aboard the spacecraft.
